intro: Mouriscas is a village in the municipality of Abrantes, in Portugal's Médio Tejo. On Rua do Mouchão, inside a low stone wall, stands an olive that a 2016 study by the University of Trás-os-Montes e Alto Douro put at about 3,350 years, one of the oldest estimates for any tree in the country. It is a Tree of Public Interest, still bears olives, and is free to see at any hour. A reader sent it to us.

question_answer: The tree to see in Mouriscas is the Olive of Mouchão, a hollow olive estimated at about 3,350 years by a 2016 study from the University of Trás-os-Montes e Alto Douro, which still bears olives beside Rua do Mouchão.
question_context: The estimate is dendrometric, read from the trunk's measurements, and a hollow olive cannot be dated by measurement alone, so the figure is one study's. The same method has put an olive in Vidigueira at more than 3,700 years. A council plaque gives a girth of 6.52 metres at chest height and 11.12 metres at the stump; the trunk is cut off a little over three metres up and the tree is about ten metres tall. It is a Galician-type olive grafted onto a wild one, still bears olives, and is reported to house a colony of bats. It has been a Tree of Public Interest since 2007 and came second in the Tree of the Year contest in 2020 and 2021. Its name comes from mouchão fishing, because fishermen gathered at the tree before going out. A stone wall and fresh soil were added around its base after the age study. It stands in a small walled public space, free to visit at any hour.

trees.story:
In 2016 a forestry scientist from the University of Trás-os-Montes e Alto Douro put this olive at about 3,350 years, give or take two percent. If that holds, it was already more than five centuries old when Rome was founded.

Hold that loosely. The method reads age from the trunk's measurements, and a hollow olive, as this one is, cannot be dated by measurement alone. So 3,350 is one study's estimate. The same university's method has put another olive near Lisbon at about 2,850 and one in Vidigueira at more than 3,700, so this is one of Portugal's oldest olives by these estimates, not the only contender.

A plaque from the Abrantes council gives 6.52 metres round at chest height and 11.12 metres at the stump. The trunk is hollowed out and cut off a little over three metres up, and from that stump the tree still grows about ten metres tall and still bears olives. It is a Galician-type olive grafted onto a wild one, and a colony of bats is reported to live in it.

The name comes from mouchão fishing. From the early twentieth century, fishermen gathered at the tree before heading out. It has been a Tree of Public Interest since 2007, came second in the Tree of the Year contest in 2020 and again in 2021, and since the age study has stood inside a stone wall with fresh soil at its feet. A reader sent it to us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow, gnarled trunk cut off just over three metres up, inside a low stone wall with a granite slab and a council plaque giving 3,350 years. It stands beside Rua do Mouchão.
trees.access: Free and open at all hours: a small walled public space beside Rua do Mouchão in Mouriscas, seen from the street. No ticket.

faq.q: How old is the Olive of Mouchão?
faq.a: About 3,350 years by a 2016 estimate from the University of Trás-os-Montes e Alto Douro, with a two percent margin. The method reads age from the trunk's size, and a hollow olive cannot be dated that way alone, so treat it as one study's figure.

faq.q: Is it the oldest tree in Portugal?
faq.a: It is one of the oldest by these estimates. The same method has put an olive in Vidigueira at more than 3,700 years.

faq.q: Can I visit the Olive of Mouchão?
faq.a: Yes, at any hour and for free. It stands inside a low stone wall in a small public space beside Rua do Mouchão in Mouriscas.
